concept.name: Illusion of control
concept.definition: The tendency to overestimate one's ability to control or influence outcomes that are partly or wholly determined by chance, named by Ellen Langer (1975). It is strengthened by 'skill cues' such as personal choice, competition, and familiarity - all abundant in trading environments.
concept.intuition: Clicking the buy button yourself, watching the screen, and having a system all feel like control over an outcome that is mostly random.
concept.mechanics: In Langer's lottery and chance-task experiments, personal choice and early success inflated perceived control over random outcomes. Fenton-O'Creevy and colleagues (2003) found that City of London traders most prone to the illusion scored significantly lower on analysis, risk management, and profit contribution.
concept.failure_modes: It inflates risk-taking because subjective risk feels lower than objective risk, and it creates insensitivity to negative feedback, impeding learning. Calibration research adds a caveat: people can also underestimate control they genuinely have.
concept.misconceptions: Feeling in control is not evidence of control; the question is whether outcomes are actually conditional on one's actions. Elaborate tooling and fast execution are skill cues that do not change the stochastic nature of returns.
concept.example: A scalper believes his rapid order flow works the market in his favor; over a year his results match a random-entry benchmark with the same risk parameters.
